To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the cross-correlation method is the best method for the detection of short-duration gravitational wave bursts; (2) the cross-correlations method and the time-frequency method are the best methods for the estimation of arrival times of short-duration gravitational waves; (3) the time-frequency method is the best for detection of long-duration gravitational wave bursts, and (4) the time-frequency and the cross-correlation methods are the best for estimating arrival times of long-duration gravitational waves.

(a) the matched-filter method is the best search for the signals considered, followed by the coherent wavelet transform, and (b) the coherent wavelet search is more robust to the presence of noise than the matched-filter method.

the two most efficient search methods are the one based on the Hough transform, which achieves 90% efficiency for a signal-to-noise ratio as low as 5.6, and the method based on the wavelet transform, which achieves the same 90% efficiency level for a signal-to noise ratio as low as ~ 5.3.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (i) Which of the search methods are most efficient at detecting gravitational wave bursts?

a comparison of the performance of the following search methods: the matched filtering method, the coherent network search method, the cross-correlation method, the coherent cross-correlation method and two methods based on the maximum likelihood method.

the following issues: (1) The comparison of the performance of the searches on the basis of the three figures of merit, (2) the comparison of the results of the searches for the same signal, (3) the study of the influence of the detector parameters on the search performance and (4) the comparison between different methods for the estimation of arrival times.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
all the methods perform well, but the method that is best for one type of signal may not be the best for other types.
all methods are competitive, and that no method stands out.
all the search algorithms are competitive and that the most appropriate choice for a particular application depends on a number of factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
all the methods are capable of detecting signals at the design sensitivities of LIGO and Virg...
the matched filter method is the most efficient search method for gravitational wave bursts, but that it is also computationally the most demanding.
the two most sensitive searches are the matched-filtering method and a new method based on a cross-correlation of two time-frequency representations of the data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the performance of the search methods varies considerably with the type of signal injected into the data.
the search methods are complementary in the sense that no one method is superior to the others for all signal types, signal-to-noise ratio ranges, and signal arrival times.
the performance of a burst search is not only a matter of the signal-to-noise ratio of the injected signal but also of the noise level of the detector and the search method employed.
